title: Queue-age charge scaling labbook: fairness vs tail stability
content:
Purpose and context

Short version: this labbook captures a sequence of experiments that add an age-derived "charge" to queued requests to bias batch formation toward older requests, with a multiplicative scaling factor that changes with queue occupancy. Goal was to reduce tail latency for long-waiting requests without catastrophically harming throughput or creating oscillation/instability in batch sizes.

Why this is different from prior work in the folder: a lot of previous notes explore deadline-based flushes, dynamic timeouts, priority demotion, or urgency-weighting. This effort treats the queue as an electrostatic system: requests accumulate charge with age, and the scheduler uses a charge-sum threshold (instead of or in addition to size/time thresholds) to trigger batch formation. Additionally, charge is scaled as a function of current headroom and recent batch success rate to avoid oscillation.

Hypotheses
- H1: Adding a per-request age charge will pull older slow-starting or preempted requests into earlier batches, lowering 95/99p latency for requests that would otherwise be starved by throughput-optimizing batching.
- H2: A naive linear charge accumulation causes batch-size oscillations under bursty arrivals; applying a queue-occupancy dependent scaling factor (damping) stabilizes batch sizes.
- H3: Charge-based triggers can be combined with soft timeouts to preserve throughput under high QPS while protecting tail latency for low-frequency, long-latency requests.

Experiment matrix (summary)
- Variables: charge accumulation slope (c0 in ms-equivalent units), charge-sum threshold (C_thr), occupancy-scaling exponent (alpha), soft-flush timeout (T_soft), max-batch-size (B_max), preemption window (P_w).
- Workloads: steady-medium (1000 rps, mean token length 48), bursty (poisson bursts to 4x for 30s every 5 min), heterogeneous-length (mixture: 70% short 16 tokens, 30% long 512 tokens), and starvation-pattern (few slow/large requests injected at low frequency).
- Hardware/bench: 4x A100 per serving pool, model: open-2-13b-quant (replicates production kernel mix), KV-cache enabled, baseline scheduler = continuous-batcher v3.4.

Representative configs tested (narrowed)
- A: c0=1.0, C_thr=200, alpha=0.0 (no scaling), T_soft=40ms, B_max=64
- B: c0=0.5, C_thr=300, alpha=0.5 (mild damping), T_soft=30ms, B_max=96
- C: c0=2.0, C_thr=150, alpha=1.0 (strong damping), T_soft=20ms, B_max=48
- D: no-charge baseline (existing prod tuning) for direct comparison

Instrumentation and new metrics
- request_age_ms recorded at enqueue and at flush
- batch_charge_sum recorded per batch (sum of age-charge at flush)
- batch_size, batch_latency (server time), end_to_end_latency (client-observed)
- size-variance over sliding 1m windows, oscillation_index = stddev(batch_size)/mean(batch_size)
- headroom_utilization = measure of free GPU slots / soft quota windows
- starvation_rate: fraction of requests > 99th baseline latency

Observations (high level)
- Baseline D: 95p = 210ms, 99p = 398ms on steady workload; bursts produce 99p spikes > 800ms.
- Config A (no damping) reduced starvation_rate by ~28% but showed high oscillation_index (0.62 -> 1.8 during burst windows). Batch sizes swung between 16 and B_max rapidly, causing throughput jitter and transient kernel underutilization.
- Config B (mild damping) achieved the best practical tradeoff: 95p reduced by ~12% relative to D, 99p reduced by ~20%, oscillation_index contained to ~0.55, throughput impact <1.7%.
- Config C (strong damping) over-prioritized age, lowering 99p for injected slow requests but increased average latency for short requests (95p for short class +9%), and reduced throughput by ~4% because batches were prematurely flushed early to capture aged requests.

Interesting micro-behaviors
- Charge saturation: when c0 and C_thr were both high, charge-sum threshold rarely hit; age charge accumulation basically acted as a time-based flush with different constants. Not helpful.
- Resonance under periodic bursts: with alpha=0, bursts created a feedback loop where earlier large batches drained queue, causing subsequent bursts to build up very fast and then flush massive single batches that created GPU pipeline stalls. Alpha>0 damped the accumulation when occupancy high, smoothing flushes.
- Interaction with KV cache: requests with warmed KV-cache tend to be shorter server time; charge-based flushing pulled them earlier into small batches more often, exposing a slight regression in average throughput. We mitigated by making charge for cache-warm requests 0.6*c0 (fluid config toggle).

Config tuning recipe (practical)
1) Start from current prod max-batch-size and soft-timeout. Set c0 to a small value (0.4--0.6 ms-equivalent) and C_thr to a value that is roughly B_max * average_age_target (empirically ~300 for our profile).
2) Enable occupancy-scaling with alpha in [0.3, 0.6]. This reduces oscillation in >60% of tested burst shapes.
3) Add class-based charge modifiers: reduce charge slope for cache-warm or short-token requests so we don't pull them out of efficient coalesced batches.
4) Observe oscillation_index for 24h; if >0.7 during bursts, increase alpha or raise C_thr.
5) If throughput drops >3% for p95-sensitive SLAs, reduce c0 and raise T_soft slightly.

Representative tracing snippet (logical)
- enqueue(req): req.age_start = now; req.charge = 0
- periodic_tick or queue_event: for queued reqs, req.charge = c0 * (now - age_start) * class_modifier
- when forming tentative batch: compute total_charge = sum(req.charge) for candidate set; flush if total_charge >= C_thr OR size >= B_max OR earliest_age > T_abs
- occupancy-scaling: effective_C_thr = C_thr * (1 + occupancy^alpha) where occupancy in [0,1]

Open issues and follow-ups
- Stability under multi-tenant mixes (different customers with different SLA priorities). Need to test whether per-tenant charge scaling interacts badly with routing/stranding.
- Formal control-theory analysis: the occupancy-scaling feels like a damping coefficient, but we should model the queue as a second-order system and derive recommended alpha bounds for guaranteed stability under bounded arrival rate changes.
- Edge-case: long-inflight KV cache fetches (blocking on remote store) create requests that accumulate disproportionate charge and get preferentially flushed, but then spend a long time in GPU due to IO. Need to incorporate estimated server-time prediction into charge (age * predicted_effort factor).
- UX controls for customers: expose a single "tail-sensitivity" knob that maps to (c0, alpha, C_thr) presets rather than raw knobs. Run a/b test on 10% of host pools.

Action items
- [Avery] implement class-based charge modifiers and hook into cache-warm signal (PR drafted: runtime#478). Target: canary on one region by 2026-03-10.
- [Sofia] build a dashboard tile for batch_charge_sum, oscillation_index, and headroom_utilization. Add alert when oscillation_index > 0.8 for >5m.
- [Jonas] run multi-tenant simulation with two synthetic tenants (high-burst vs steady) over 72h and submit logs; priority: understand cross-tenant starvation.
- [Riley] schedule control-theory brainstorming session with SRE to map out stability bounds (2h).

Notes to self / scratch ideas
- Consider exponential decay on per-request charge after being deferred N times (prevent permanent priority inversion of frequent short requests).
- Maybe combine with probabilistic admission: cap number of high-charge requests that can be scheduled simultaneously to avoid too many long jobs occupying GPU pool.
- Track per-model charge profiles; larger models might need different c0 scaling (per-param multiplier).

Appendix: quick numbers table (selected runs)
- D baseline: steady: p95=210ms p99=398ms throughput=1000 rps nominal
- A no damping: steady: p95=190ms p99=320ms throughput=995 rps oscillation_index=1.1
- B mild damping: steady: p95=185ms p99=318ms throughput=984 rps oscillation_index=0.55
- C strong damping: steady: p95=205ms p99=270ms throughput=960 rps oscillation_index=0.42

If this looks promising we can fold the mild-damping preset into the next canary and monitor the dashboard metrics above. Document intentionally includes rough numbers and heuristic thresholds — next step is formal sweep and SLO mapping.

End of labbook entry (version 0.9)
